renown

/rih-NOWN/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Renown means widespread fame combined with a good reputation.

The marine biologist's renown grew with every reef her team brought back from the brink.

Worked Example

The community orchestra in Dover Falls rehearsed in a church basement for thirty years. Then a recording of their winter concert spread among conductors, and invitations began arriving — first from the state capital, then from festivals abroad. By the time the players packed for their first international tour, the little orchestra's renown had outgrown the town on its own bus-stop sign.

The invitations spreading from the capital to festivals abroad show the orchestra's name traveling far beyond its home with an excellent reputation attached — that widespread, earned fame is renown.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

fame: Fame is simply the state of being widely known — for anything at all, good, bad, or trivial. Renown is fame of a particular kind: the name travels far and carries an excellent reputation with it. A scandal can bring fame overnight; renown has to be earned.

prominence: Prominence means being important and noticeable — standing out where everyone can see you, a name always in the headlines. Renown does not need the spotlight: it is measured by how far and how favorably a name travels, and it can build quietly for decades.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

obscurity: the state of being unknown

anonymity: the state of being nameless to the public

Where it sits · how far and how long fame travels — recognition → renown → immortality

recognition vs. renown: Recognition means people know your name; renown means your name travels widely and carries an excellent reputation with it.

immortality vs. renown: Immortality goes past renown — fame so lasting that the name outlives its owner by centuries.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — re-

Prefix — re-: again and again (Latin)

Root — nown

Root — nown: to name (Latin nominare, via Old French nomer)

Put it together

Put it together: Renown travels from Latin nominare, 'to name' — the root of nominate, nominee, and noun — through Old French renomer, 'to name again and again.' That is precisely what renown is: a name spoken over and over, in more and more places, with respect attached each time it is repeated.

Use the root in a new word: nominee

Use the root in a new word: nominee: A nominee is someone officially named for an honor — the same Latin root nominare, 'to name,' that gives the repeatedly-named their renown.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal, literary; neutral-to-positive

Renown is earned, wide, and respectable fame — keep it apart from this unit's other praise words: adulation is gushing admiration aimed at you, a commendation is one official document of praise, and idolatrous describes worship gone too far, while renown simply measures how far and how favorably your name has traveled.
